data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"City size is the single best modulator: larger cities accumulate more total thermal storage and anthropogenic heat, producing a larger nocturnal gap that scales with the urban diameter.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If heat advection from the surroundings or boundary layer dynamics dominate over internal thermal storage, city size scaling fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the nocturnal gap is determined by local urban density (SVF) rather than total extent, city size is a proxy rather than the causal mechanism.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If population density is uniformly high regardless of size, the scaling with size may break down.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The nocturnal UHI is driven by the total thermal energy retained in the urban environment, comprising both daytime heat storage and anthropogenic emissions. City size (diameter or total area) controls the total volume of the urban heat reservoir. A larger city has more impervious surface area to absorb solar radiation and more building mass to store it. After sunset, this larger stored energy reservoir releases sensible heat, maintaining higher air temperatures. The nocturnal gap scales with city size because the total thermal inertia of the system is proportional to its physical extent.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
